title: Clinging
hook: holding on to God through the whole day

segments.voice: Yesterday, no place without God: from Jacob's stone pillow to the bus stop. Your line was no place without him. Where did you say, even here? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

A small child crossing a busy street holds a parent's hand. The child isn't thinking about the hand the whole time. They're chatting, pointing at a dog, counting buses. But the hand never lets go. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day." Cleave. Hold fast. The Torah asks for it more than once. The rabbis, and later the Hasidic teachers, asked the obvious question: how does a person do that, all day long, in the middle of everything else? Today's word.
screen: `A HAND ACROSS THE STREET.` → `YE THAT DID CLEAVE.` → `HOW, ALL DAY LONG?`

segments.voice: Devekut. Clinging, attachment, holding on to God. Turn it four ways. First, the problem. The Torah tells the people to cleave to God. But the Talmud raises an objection. The Torah also describes God as a fire that consumes. How can anyone hold on to a fire? Second, the rabbis' answers. In one passage, the Talmud says: walk after God's ways. As God clothed the naked, clothe the naked. As God visited the sick, visit the sick. As God comforted mourners and buried the dead, do the same. In another passage, the answer is to attach yourself to the wise, to stand close to people who live by the Torah and help them. Either way, clinging to God turns into something your hands do. Third, the Hasidic turn. Hasidic teachers made devekut a center of the spiritual life, and they refused to keep it inside the synagogue. Hold on to God while praying, yes, and also while eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. Yesterday's line, no place without God, is what makes that possible. If God is in every place, then every place is somewhere to hold on. Fourth, the hand. Devekut doesn't ask a person to stop living and stare at heaven. Like the child on the street, attention can wander to a dog or a bus while the hold stays firm. A hand can slip. The practice is to notice, and take hold again. So clinging, in this tradition, is less like a grip of fear and more like walking with someone you trust, all the way across.
screen: `HOW DO YOU HOLD A FIRE?` · `WALK IN GOD'S WAYS.` · `IN EVERY PLACE, HOLD ON.` · `WHEN THE HAND SLIPS, TAKE HOLD.` · then, large: `CLING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember God during one chore. Choose a chore you could do now, or one you'll do later: washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter. Settle, and breathe. If you can, do it now, slowly. If not, picture doing it. As your hands work, keep one thread of attention on God, or, if that word doesn't fit you, on what you're grateful for. Not thinking hard. Just holding on, the way a hand is held crossing the street. When your mind wanders, come back to the thread. The bell holds the time.
Devekut. Clinging: holding on to God through the whole day, in prayer, in kindness and in ordinary work. Today's word.
Your line: cling. Today, during one chore, hold on to God, or to gratitude, the whole way through, the way you'd hold a hand crossing a street. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: In Hasidic teaching, devekut is pursued in prayer and also in daily activities such as eating, work and conversation, while the Talmud's teaching to walk in God's ways is lived through acts like visiting the sick and comforting mourners.

fork.setup: the Torah tells you to cleave to God, but it also calls God a consuming fire. how does the Talmud say you can hold on?
options: you can't: the command is only for angels.
walk in God's ways: clothe the naked, visit the sick, comfort mourners.
stay away from people and think only of God.
fork.reveal: as God clothed the naked and visited the sick, the Talmud says, so you do the same: clinging becomes kindness.

notes: Editor pass: cut the unsourced claim that the teachers 'admitted the hand slips'; removed 'and it will', which told the listener what they will do.
Deuteronomy 4:4 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm wording.

Sotah 14a paraphrased: how can one walk after God, who is a consuming fire? Walk after His attributes: clothe the naked, visit the sick, comfort mourners, bury the dead. Ketubot 111b paraphrased: how can one cleave to God? Cleave to Torah scholars (marry into their families, do business for them, benefit them). Please confirm both; Sotah 14a is framed around 'walking after' and Ketubot 111b around 'cleaving'.
'The Torah asks for it more than once' rests on Deuteronomy 11:22, 13:5 and 30:20; please confirm verse numbers (13:5 in JPS numbering).
Hasidic devekut in daily activity is stated generally; 'the teachers who wrote about it admitted the hand slips' is a general claim and may need a source or softening.
